To date, Japan’s peaceful nuclear energy use has taken the form of a nuclear fuel recycling policy that reprocesses spent fuel and effectively utilizes the plutonium retrieved in light water reactors (LWRs) and fast reactors (FRs). With the aim to complete recycling domestically, Japan has introduced key technology from abroad and has further developed its own technology and industry. However, Japan presently seems to have issues regarding its recycling policy and plutonium management.

![](https://fas.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/shutterstock_188616788.jpeg)

Image courtesy of Shutterstock

Because of recent increasing risks of terrorism and nuclear proliferation in the world, the international community seeks much more secure use of nuclear energy. All of the countries that store plutonium (which can be used for making nuclear weapons) must make the best efforts possible to decrease it. Taking this into account, concerns about Japan’s problem of plutonium management have been growing in the international community and Japan’s accountability for its recycling policy is essential.

In this paper, Yusei Nagata, an FAS Research Fellow from MEXT, Japan, analyzes U.S. experts’ opinions and concerns about Japan’s problem and considers what Japan can (and should) do to solve it.

A "**nuclear umbrella**" is a guarantee by a [nuclear-weapon state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_with_nuclear_weapons "List of states with nuclear weapons") to defend a non-nuclear [allied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance "Alliance") state. The context is usually the [security alliances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_alliance "Security alliance") of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") with [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"),[[1]](#cite_note-:4-1) [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"),[[2]](#cite_note-2) [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"),[[3]](#cite_note-:3-3) the [North Atlantic Treaty Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty_Organization "North Atlantic Treaty Organization") (much of [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") and [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada")) and the [Compact of Free Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_of_Free_Association "Compact of Free Association") (the [Federated States of Micronesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federated_States_of_Micronesia "Federated States of Micronesia"), the [Marshall Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Islands "Marshall Islands"), and [Palau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palau "Palau")). Those alliances were formed because of the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") and the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). For some countries, it was an alternative to acquiring nuclear weapons themselves; other alternatives include regional [nuclear-weapon-free zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear-weapon-free_zone "Nuclear-weapon-free zone") or [nuclear sharing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_sharing "Nuclear sharing"). Nuclear umbrellas are also referred to as "**extended deterrence**" under which a nuclear-weapon state extends its [nuclear deterrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_deterrence "Nuclear deterrence") to cover threats against its non-nuclear-weapon state allies.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## United States-provided

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_umbrella&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: United States-provided")]

The United States has promised its role as a "nuclear umbrella" for numerous non-nuclear allied states, even as early as the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War").[[1]](#cite_note-:4-1) The US now has security alliances of this nature with around 30 countries, many within NATO itself.[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5) The country also has notable arrangements of this type with South Korea[[3]](#cite_note-:3-3) and Australia.[[1]](#cite_note-:4-1) The US understood the power of deterrence with nuclear weapons early on, beginning with the concept of massive retaliation during the [Eisenhower administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenhower_administration "Eisenhower administration").[[6]](#cite_note-:5-6) As the USSR and other countries became nuclear powers as well, however, the risk of any nuclear exchange became more clear.[[6]](#cite_note-:5-6) This, in part, motivated the US to adopt the new strategy of deterrence, in which they would have more control over the situation, while still maintaining the ability to intervene in conflicts, a nuclear umbrella.[[6]](#cite_note-:5-6) The US provides protection and deterrence for various countries under its umbrella, and in turn, the countries do not pursue nuclear weapons programs themselves.[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5) More recently, however, concerns have been raised about the diminishing power of such a threat, due to the rapid increase of nuclear [weapons of mass destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapon_of_mass_destruction "Weapon of mass destruction") across the globe.[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5) Russia in particular has caused concern, having focused their military doctrine on nuclear weapons, as well as continued in the development of their weapons programs.[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5) Currently, the United States holds only some "nonstrategic" military weapons in Europe, and these nonstrategic weapons aid in reassuring countries under the umbrella, and emphasizing their role as a deterrent.[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5) The strategy of deterrence remains unequivocally important for the country, but many argue that the US will face various new challenges when it comes to the rise of other nuclear powers and weapons of mass destruction.[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5)

The number of seniors in Japan, aged 65 or over, as of September 15, 2023, stood at 36.2 million, according to data from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications. This was a year-on-year fall of 10,000, the first such decline since comparable data became available in 1950. Overall, though, the ratio of seniors within the total population increased by 0.1 percentage points to 29.1%, making it the highest on record.

[![Japan’s Population by Age Group](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2474038/2474038.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2474038/2474038.png)

Senior population statistics show that there were 20.5 million women (32.1% of the total population) and 15.7 million men (26.0%), meaning women exceeded men by 4.8 million.

The population of those in their seventies and over rose by 200,000 to 28.9 million, a 0.2-point increase from the previous year to 23.2%. This equates to one in four women and one in five men who are 70 or over.

The number of seniors aged 75 and over increased by 720,000 to 20.1 million, the first time the figure has exceeded 20 million. This sector of the population was 16.1%, a year-on-year 0.6-percentage point increase. As of 2022, the substantial cohort of Japanese baby boomers (born between 1947 and 1949) began reaching the age of 75 and is growing significantly.

According to United Nations data, Japan’s senior population ratio (the ratio of people aged 65 and over) of 29.1% puts it well ahead of Italy, in second place with 24.5%.

As of September 1, 2023, there were 92,139 centenarians in Japan, an increase of 1,613 from the previous year, according to resident registration data. This is the fifty-third annual rise in people aged 100 or over. Japan is well-known for its long life expectancy and women account for the majority of centenarians with a ratio of 88.5%.

[![Number of Centenarians and Average Lifespan](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2470431/2470431.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2470431/2470431.png)

Japan’s oldest woman is 116-year-old Tatsumi Fusa, who lives in Kashiwara, Osaka Prefecture. The oldest man in Japan is Sonobe Gisaburō, aged 111 and living in Tateyama, Chiba Prefecture.

In 1963, when the government enacted the Act on Social Welfare for the Elderly, there were 153 Japanese centenarians nationwide. That figure passed the 1,000 mark in 1981, topped 10,000 in 1998, and since then has continued to rise steadily.

The prefecture with the highest ratio of centenarians per 100,000 population was Shimane at 155.2, which was almost 3.5 times as many as that of the lowest, Saitama with 44.8. Western Japan tends to have higher ratios than the east of the country, and there are particularly low figures in the Kantō region, centered on Tokyo, and other urban areas.

The **49th G7 summit** was held from 19 to 21 May 2023 in the city of [Hiroshima](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima") in [Hiroshima Prefecture](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Prefecture "Hiroshima Prefecture").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Leaders of [G7](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") countries joined in Hiroshima to discuss a number of challenges to peace and prosperity facing the global order while consulting with invited guests. The issues discussed included the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine") and effects on the international order, [climate change](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), the [COVID-19 pandemic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), and other geopolitical crises. To resolve these issues, the G7 pledged to uphold the free and open international order based on "the rule of law", and strengthened the G7's outreach to emerging and developing countries.[[4]](#cite_note-JF_2023-05-13-4)

The long invitees list reflects attempts to influence the "[Global South](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_South "Global South")", a term used for developing countries in [Asia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia"), [Africa](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") and [Latin America](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), all of which have complex political and economic ties to both [Russia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") and [China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China").[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Many geopolitical commentators[*[who?](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")*] remarked that Ukrainian President [Volodymyr Zelenskyy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volodymyr_Zelenskyy "Volodymyr Zelenskyy") received much attention and dominated the summit,[[6]](#cite_note-6) and that the Hiroshima summit achieved many objectives.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

The leaders' communiqué featured commitments and statements on a range of topics including climate, health, [food security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_security "Food security"), and technology. However, the Russian invasion of Ukraine, [nuclear nonproliferation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_proliferation "Nuclear proliferation"), and [economic security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_security "Economic security") were the most prominent.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-G7-LC-9) Other five standalone statements were issued.[[10]](#cite_note-LSU_2023-05-19-10)[[11]](#cite_note-LHVND_2023-05-19-11)[[12]](#cite_note-G7-ER&ES-12)[[13]](#cite_note-CEEAP_2023-05-20-13)[[14]](#cite_note-RGFS_2023-05-20-14)

In not one but two statements, the G7 made clear to China their stance on divisive geopolitical hot spots such as the [Indo-Pacific](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pacific "Indo-Pacific") and [Taiwan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), but the most important part of their message centered on what they called "economic coercion".[[15]](#cite_note-BBC_2023-05-21-15)[[16]](#cite_note-VOA_2023-05-21-16)[[12]](#cite_note-G7-ER&ES-12)

[Fumio Kishida](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumio_Kishida "Fumio Kishida") chaired the 49th G7 summit.

All G7 member states participated, including the representatives of the [European Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"). International organizations, such as the [United Nations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") (UN) and [World Trade Organization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Organization "World Trade Organization") (WTO) were also in attendance.[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Following [Russia's invasion of Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine") in February 2022, G7 member states heavily sanctioned Russia, which was [a member until 2014](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Crimea_by_the_Russian_Federation "Annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation"), with some arming the [Ukrainian military](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_Ukraine "Armed Forces of Ukraine") with weapons.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was invited to a virtual summit meeting of G7 leaders, which was held on 24 February 2023, the first anniversary of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

Japan held the presidency of the G7 for 2023, and in an attempt to reach to the "[Global South](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_North_and_Global_South "Global North and Global South")" of nations, [Japanese Prime Minister](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Japan "Prime Minister of Japan") [Fumio Kishida](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumio_Kishida "Fumio Kishida") invited the leaders of [Australia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), [Brazil](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [Comoros](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comoros "Comoros"), [Cook Islands](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_Islands "Cook Islands"), [India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Indonesia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), [South Korea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), and [Vietnam](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam").[[19]](#cite_note-NHK_2023-02-21-19)[[20]](#cite_note-Yomiuri_2023-03-21-20)[[21]](#cite_note-:0-21) All nations accepted the invitations, with India hosting the [2023 G20 New Delhi summit](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_G20_New_Delhi_summit "2023 G20 New Delhi summit").[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The 2023 summit was the first summit for [British Prime Minister](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") [Rishi Sunak](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak "Rishi Sunak") and [Italian Prime Minister](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Italy "Prime Minister of Italy") [Giorgia Meloni](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgia_Meloni "Giorgia Meloni").[[22]](#cite_note-GU_2023-05-18-22)[[23]](#cite_note-Politico_2023-05-20-23)[[24]](#cite_note-Yom_20230-5-21-24)

The **Hiroshima AI Process** is an international initiative launched by the [Group of Seven](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Seven "Group of Seven") (G7) in 2023 to coordinate approaches to the governance of advanced and generative [artificial intelligence](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"). It was established at the [49th G7 summit](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_G7_summit "49th G7 summit") in [Hiroshima](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima"), Japan, as a forum for international discussion of risks, standards, and policy responses related to rapidly developing AI technologies.[[1]](#cite_note-Reuters2023-1)

The initiative has been described as part of wider competition among major economies to shape global AI governance and harmonise regulatory approaches.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

The Hiroshima AI Process was initiated amid increasing international concern about the rapid development of generative AI systems and the lack of coordinated global regulatory approaches. At the 2023 G7 summit in Hiroshima, leaders agreed to establish a ministerial-level process to examine governance challenges posed by advanced AI and to develop shared approaches to standards and risk management.[[1]](#cite_note-Reuters2023-1)

The initiative emerged alongside other international efforts focused on AI governance, including work associated with the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development "Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development") (OECD) and policy initiatives in the [European Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## Development and objectives

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hiroshima_AI_Process&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Development and objectives")]

The Hiroshima AI Process functions as an ongoing framework for dialogue among G7 members and partners regarding the safe and trustworthy development of advanced AI systems. Policy analysts have described its aims as promoting international coordination, encouraging transparency, and developing shared governance principles for emerging AI technologies.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In October 2023, G7 leaders agreed on international guiding principles and a voluntary code of conduct for organisations developing advanced AI systems under the process.[[6]](#cite_note-ReutersCode-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Inflation is pushing a movement among companies to boost wages to secure workers. In fiscal 2022, one in four of Japan’s listed companies raised annual salaries by more than ¥300,000.

The average annual salary for 3,800 listed companies in Japan in fiscal 2022 (April 2022–March 2023) rose year-on-year by ¥140,000, or 2.2%, to ¥6.4 million. This was approximately ¥2 million higher than the overall average annual salary in Japan, which stands at ¥4,430,000. Both the average salary at listed companies and the amount of the increase were the highest on record over the last twenty years. The median was ¥6.1 million; the first time that it has surpassed the ¥6 million mark.

[![Average Salaries at Listed Companies by Fiscal Year](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2440413/2440413.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2440413/2440413.png)

Average salaries at 68.9% of listed companies increased from the previous year, indicating that momentum to raise pay is steadily spreading. One in four listed companies (25.3%) increased salaries by ¥300,000 or more and half (52.1%) raised them by more than ¥100,000. The push to increase pay due to rising prices and labor shortages is thought to be behind this sharp rise from fiscal 2022 onward.

The most common range for average salaries with 27.7% (1,059 companies), was ¥5 million up to ¥6 million, followed by 24.5% in the ¥6 million to ¥7 million range, and 19.4% paying between ¥4 million and ¥5 million. There was a 20-year record high of 134 companies that paid average salaries of more than ¥10 million. This included general trading companies, M&A brokers, media companies, and real estate agents. The salaries at roughly 90% of all the listed companies were higher than the national average.

Contained entirely within [Shiga Prefecture](https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/pref25/), it is three times the size of Lake Kasumigaura, which with a surface area of 220 square kilometers is the second largest in the country. The number of gas stations in Japan at the end of fiscal 2022 stood at 27,963, according to the Agency for Natural Resources and Energy. This was a decrease of 512 from the previous year. In 2002, there were more than 50,000 gas stations, meaning the number has fallen by more than 40% over the past 20 years.

[![Number of Gas Stations and Self-Service Gas Stations](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2496240/2496240.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2496240/2496240.png)

Increased efforts toward fuel efficiency and decarbonization leading to a drop in demand for gasoline are thought to be one factor behind the decline, alongside a lack of people in rural areas who can continue managing gas stations. There were numerous cases where gas stations closed down rather than investing such a large amount of capital, due to falling profits and the fact the owners were getting on in age.

This decline in gas stations has led to major issues in rural areas, including “the distance between home and the gas station being too far” and “causing problems delivering kerosene to seniors who have no means of transport.” According to the agency, as of the end of fiscal 2021, there were 282 municipalities across the country where the distance by road from people’s residences to the nearest gas station was at least 15 kilometers.

At the end of fiscal 2012, the agency started to publish the number of municipalities with three or fewer gas stations. There were 348 such municipalities as of fiscal 2021, of which 10 had none at all.

The chart below shows that these municipalities are distributed relatively evenly across Japan. By prefecture, Hokkaidō had the most with 65. This was followed by 35 in Nagano and 20 in Nara. In contrast, Tochigi and Ibaraki had none.

The **Bank of Japan** (日本銀行, *Nippon Ginkō*; **BOJ**) is the [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank") of [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan").[[4]](#cite_note-nussbaum708-5) The bank is often called *Nichigin* (日銀) for short. It is headquartered in [Nihonbashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihonbashi "Nihonbashi"), Chūō, Tokyo.[[5]](#cite_note-6)

The said bank is a corporate entity independent of the [Japanese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Japan "Government of Japan"),[[1]](#cite_note-outline-1) and while it is not an [administrative organisation of the state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_organisation "Administrative organisation"), its [monetary policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_policy "Monetary policy") falls within the scope of administration. From a [macroeconomic perspective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroeconomics "Macroeconomics"), long-term stability of prices is deemed crucial. However, the political sector tends to favour short-term measures. Thus, the bank's autonomy and independence are granted from the standpoint of ensuring long-term public welfare and political neutrality.[[6]](#cite_note-7)

Like most modern Japanese institutions, the Bank of Japan was founded after the [Meiji Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Restoration "Meiji Restoration"). Prior to the Restoration, Japan's feudal fiefs all issued their own money, *[hansatsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrip_of_Edo_period_Japan "Scrip of Edo period Japan")*, in an array of incompatible denominations, but the *New Currency Act* of Meiji 4 (1871) did away with these and established the [yen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yen "Yen") as the new decimal currency, which had parity with the Mexican silver dollar.[[7]](#cite_note-8) The former [han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_(Japan) "Han (Japan)") (fiefs) became [prefectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefectures_of_Japan "Prefectures of Japan") and their mints became private chartered banks which, however, initially retained the right to print money. For a time both the central government and these so-called [national banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Banks_in_Meiji_Japan "National Banks in Meiji Japan") issued money.

### Foundation and early development

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bank_of_Japan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Foundation and early development")]

Finance minister [Matsukata Masayoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsukata_Masayoshi "Matsukata Masayoshi") initially proposed the creation of the bank of Japan sometime in March 1882, soon enacted in the Bank of Japan Act (Imperial Ordinance) of 27 June 1882 and formally founded on 10 October 1882.[[8]](#cite_note-Metzler-9): 25 The primary source of inspiration for the bank's design was the [National Bank of Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bank_of_Belgium "National Bank of Belgium") (est. 1850) which was viewed as one of the best-designed European [central banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank") of its era.[[9]](#cite_note-10) Since then, the Bank of Japan has been partly privately owned. **Kazuo Ueda** ([Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 植田 和男, [Hepburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *Ueda Kazuo*; born September 20, 1951) is a Japanese economist who has been serving as the 32nd Governor of the [Bank of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Japan "Bank of Japan") (BOJ) since April 2023.

He is a [professor emeritus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professor_emeritus "Professor emeritus") at the [University of Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tokyo "University of Tokyo") (UTokyo) and also worked briefly as a professor at [Kyoritsu Women’s University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoritsu_Women's_University "Kyoritsu Women's University") after his retirement from UTokyo in 2017. He was the dean of the [Faculty of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Economics,_University_of_Tokyo "Faculty of Economics, University of Tokyo") at UTokyo and president of the Japanese Economic Association.

Ueda graduated from the University of Tokyo with a Bachelor of Science in Mathematics and then studied at Faculty of Economics under [Hirofumi Uzawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirofumi_Uzawa "Hirofumi Uzawa"), [Ryutaro Komiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryutaro_Komiya?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ryutaro Komiya (page does not exist)"), and [Koichi Hamada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koichi_Hamada_(economist) "Koichi Hamada (economist)").[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Nikkei_2011-10-21-2) In 1980, Ueda received his PhD in economics from the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology").[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) His doctoral advisor was [Stanley Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Fischer "Stanley Fischer").

After working at the [University of British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_British_Columbia "University of British Columbia") and [Osaka University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka_University "Osaka University"), he returned to his alma mater in 1989, retiring in 2017 to become Professor Emeritus.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) From April 2011 to June 2012, Ueda was president of the [Japan Economic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Economic_Association "Japanese Economic Association").[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

In February 2023, Ueda was nominated by Prime Minister [Fumio Kishida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumio_Kishida "Fumio Kishida") to succeed the long-serving [Haruhiko Kuroda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haruhiko_Kuroda "Haruhiko Kuroda") as Governor of the Bank of Japan. He was an unexpected choice as the position is usually filled by a senior official from the [Ministry of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Finance_(Japan) "Ministry of Finance (Japan)") or the bank itself. Ueda began his term in April 2023.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) On 19 March 2024, the BoJ under Ueda decided to end the zero-interest-rate policy and the yield curve control.[[5]](#cite_note-d566-5) This was a milestone for the long-stagnant Japanese economy, as the bank rate had not been raised for 17 years due to deflation or very low inflation, which the country finally got out of with the help of the [2021-2023 global inflation surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932023_inflation_surge "2021–2023 inflation surge").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

On the morning of 14 June 2023, a shooting occurred at a military training center of [Japan Ground Self-Defense Force](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Ground_Self-Defense_Force "Japan Ground Self-Defense Force") in [Gifu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gifu "Gifu"), [Gifu Prefecture](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gifu_Prefecture "Gifu Prefecture"), central [Japan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan").[[1]](#cite_note-1) A cadet allegedly opened fire on his colleagues during a live-fire training exercise, resulting in the deaths of two people and the injury of a third. The 18-year-old suspect Naoto Watanabe (渡辺直杜) was arrested.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The incident took place at the Hino Basic Shooting Range, located about 7 km east of [JR Tokai](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Japan_Railway_Company "Central Japan Railway Company") [Gifu Station](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B2%90%E9%98%9C%E9%A7%85 "ja:岐阜駅"), which was established in 1907 as a firing range for the [68th Infantry Regiment](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%AD%A9%E5%85%B5%E7%AC%AC68%E9%80%A3%E9%9A%8A "ja:歩兵第68連隊") of the [Imperial Japanese Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Japanese_Army "Imperial Japanese Army") and has been used by the [Japan Ground Self-Defense Force](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Ground_Self-Defense_Force "Japan Ground Self-Defense Force") since 1960. Originally an open-air firing range, the area was converted to an indoor firing range in 2015 due to the development of residential areas in the vicinity.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

On the day of the incident, live-fire training for the education of new cadets was being conducted from around 9:00 a.m., and this was the last day of firing training.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Naoto Watanabe (then 18 years old), one of the self-defense cadets, was working with other cadets at a place called the "preparation line" located in front of the firing position, receiving live ammunition and putting it into the magazine under the instructor's instruction, when he suddenly loaded his gun without permission. Sergeant Kosuke Yashiro[[8]](#cite_note-8) (then 25 years old), who was in charge of the waiting area, noticed this and instructed Watanabe to stop moving. At around 9:08, Watanabe fired at Sgt. Kosuke Yashiro with a [Type 89 5.56mm rifle](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howa_Type_89 "Howa Type 89"), and then turned toward Master Sgt. Yasuchika Kikumatsu (he was 52 years old[[9]](#cite_note-9)), who was in charge of the "ammunitions staff" that managed and delivered live ammunition in the back. He then turned around and fired at Yasuchika Kikumatsu, who was in charge of managing and receiving live ammunition behind him, and fired at Yusuke Hara. Kosuke Yashiro was hit in the side, Yasuchika Kikumatsu was hit twice in the chest, and Yusuke Hara was hit in the left thigh.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-:1-12) Sergeant Yusuke Hara was seriously injured with a total recovery of three months.[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) Sergeants Kosuke Yashiro and Yasuchika Kikumatsu who died and Sergeant Yusuke Hara who was seriously injured were all assigned to [Moriyama Garrison](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%AE%88%E5%B1%B1%E9%A7%90%E5%B1%AF%E5%9C%B0 "ja:守山駐屯地").

After the assault, the suspect sought refuge within the residence of Nakano City Assembly speaker, Masamichi Aoki.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) During the siege that followed, two relatives of the suspect, including his mother, managed to escape from the home. He was later apprehended and identified as Aoki's son at 4:37 A.M. the next day.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

A woman in her 40s and two police officers, aged 46 and 61, were killed in the attack. The motive behind his actions remains unclear.[[11]](#cite_note-11) When questioned by a witness about the reason for stabbing the woman, the suspect allegedly responded, "I killed her because I wanted to." He later stated that he thought the women he killed were talking badly of him during a police interrogation.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Masamichi Aoki, the speaker for the Nakano City Assembly, resigned the day his son was arrested.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

At his trial, Aoki's lawyers argued that had "diminished capacity" because of schizophrenia and called for him to receive a life sentence. On October 14, 2025, he was sentenced to death for the murders.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Following the arrest, residents of the area were initially compelled to find alternative accommodations for the night, and the local school remained closed.[[15]](#cite_note-15) However, once the arrest took place, authorities informed the community that they were free to resume their daily activities.

The **My Number Card** ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): マイナンバーカード, [Hepburn](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *mai nanbā kādo*), officially **Individual Number Card** ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 個人番号カード, [Hepburn](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *kojin bangō kādo*), is an [identity document](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_document "Identity document") issued to citizens of [Japan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and foreign residents which contains a unique 12-digit [Individual Number](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_Number "Individual Number") ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 個人番号, [Hepburn](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *kojin bangō*) that serves as a [national identification number](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_identification_number "National identification number") in Japan.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Unlike similar-looking [identity cards in Europe](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_identity_cards_in_the_European_Economic_Area_and_Switzerland "National identity cards in the European Economic Area and Switzerland"), the My Number Card can be issued to both Japanese citizens and foreign residents, and is not proof of nationality. The My Number Card is used in Japan to streamline administrative purposes like filing taxes and social security, and it is also utilized to provide disaster response to those in need. It is the [de facto](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto "De facto") Japanese equivalent to a U.S. [Social Security Number](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_number "Social Security number").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The My Number Card stores information such as personal name, photo, address, birthday, and sex. Residents who wish to obtain the card can request an application form from the municipality (via a ward office or city hall) where they reside.

Many countries around the world, including Japan, require residents and citizens to [disclose and register their address with the government](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resident_registration "Resident registration") for various bureaucratic purposes. Many countries obligate that their residents and citizens provide up to date information regarding [where they reside](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domicile_(law) "Domicile (law)"), by visiting a [registration office](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registration_office "Registration office") or the [police](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police "Police") within a few days after establishing a new residence. However some countries, like the United States or Canada, do not require their residents or citizens to provide this information to the government, unless they are applying for a passport or drivers license.

Both Japanese citizens and foreign residents are obligated to report their [domicile](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domicile_(law) "Domicile (law)") to their nearest municipal government office.

The **health care system in Japan** provides different types of services, including screening examinations, [prenatal care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prenatal_care "Prenatal care") and [infectious disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infectious_disease "Infectious disease") control, with the patient accepting responsibility for 30% of these costs while the government pays the remaining 70%. Payment for personal medical services is offered by a [universal health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care") insurance system that provides relative equality of access, with fees set by a government committee. All residents of [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") are required by the law to have health insurance coverage. People without employer insurance; insurance provided by the employer, where premiums are split between the employer and employee, can participate in a national [health insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_insurance "Health insurance") program, administered by local governments. Patients are free to select physicians or facilities of their choice and cannot be denied coverage.

Medical fees are strictly regulated by the government to keep them affordable. Depending on the family's income and the age of the insured, patients are responsible for paying 10%, 20%, or 30% of medical fees, with the government paying the remaining fee.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Also, monthly thresholds are set for each household, again depending on income and age, and medical fees exceeding the threshold are waived or reimbursed by the government.

Uninsured patients are responsible for paying 100% of their medical fees, but fees are waived for low-income households receiving a government subsidy.

In 1961, Japan achieved universal health insurance coverage, and almost everyone became insured. However, the copayment rates differed greatly.
